sre-vs-ops.cap: An ops team grows with the service. %1% caps operational work at 50%, so the engineering half compounds into automation and self-healing systems.
nines.cap: Each extra nine cuts allowed downtime by 10×. Above three nines a human cannot reliably detect, decide and act inside the budget, so the response has to be automated.
sli-slo-sla.cap: The %1% measures, the %2% targets, the %3% promises with consequences. Keep the %4% stricter than the %5%: the buffer absorbs measurement noise and gives you time to react before a contract is breached.
error-budget.cap: A 30-day %1% being consumed. Burn rate is how many times faster than the pace that would exhaust the budget exactly at day 30. One incident took 45% of the budget in two hours, a %2% near 160×.
golden-signals.cap: The four %1%, with the %2% metric that usually carries each one. Page on latency and errors, which users feel; use traffic and saturation to explain what you see.
golden-signals.leading-indicator-of-the: leading indicator of the other three
golden-signals.how-full-the-constrained: how full the constrained resource is
golden-signals.split-fast-errors-from: split fast errors from slow successes
burn-rate.cap: Multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerting. Each rule fires only when both its windows exceed the threshold: the long window proves the burn is significant, the short window proves it is still happening, so the alert clears soon after a fix. Burn rate is the observed error rate divided by the rate that would spend the whole budget over the 30-day window.
burn-rate.fire-only-when-both: fire only when BOTH windows exceed the threshold
automation-ladder.cap: The evolution of automation. Each rung moves the human further from the loop: from running every command by hand, through shared tooling, to systems that detect and fix their own failures, and finally to designs where the failure mode no longer exists.
automation-ladder.no-automation-needed-t: no automation needed — the failure mode is gone
automation-ladder.internal-system-specif: internal, system-specific — it detects and fixes itself
automation-ladder.external-system-specif: external, system-specific scripts — run by hand
automation-ladder.no-automation-a-human: no automation — a human runs every step
canary.cap: Progressive rollout. Each stage is gated on a bake time plus an %1% comparison between the %2% and a concurrently running baseline. Any failed gate rolls back automatically to the previous version.
troubleshooting-loop.cap: The hypothetico-deductive troubleshooting loop. Triage stops the bleeding before diagnosis begins; a rejected hypothesis sends you back for more data; a cure ends in a written %1% or %2%.
ics.cap: Incident command roles. The Incident Commander coordinates and decides but never debugs; if they start debugging, they hand command over first. Roles are not people: one person may hold several early on.
lb-tiers.cap: Load balancing happens at four tiers. Each balances a different unit and sees different information: %1% picks a region, the edge picks a target, the client picks among a subset, and the backend reports how loaded it is.
lb-tiers.healthy-refusing-draining-unhea: healthy / refusing (draining) / unhealthy · reports utilisation upward
lb-tiers.subsetting-weighted-round-robin: subsetting · weighted round robin by reported utilisation · %1%
lb-tiers.nlb-flow-hash-alb: %1% flow hash · %2% round robin or least outstanding → picks a target
lb-tiers.route-53-latency-or: %1% latency or geo routing · %2% anycast → picks a region
cascade.cap: The cascading-failure feedback loop: one overloaded replica dies, its load shifts to the survivors, clients retry, and the next one dies. Every arrow is a place to break the cycle.
quorum.cap: Majority %1% with five replicas. Any two majorities overlap in at least one node, so two conflicting values can never both be committed. Five replicas tolerate two failures, three tolerate one, and even counts add cost without adding tolerance.
data-defense.cap: Defense in depth for data integrity. Soft deletion catches user and application mistakes, backups catch corruption and region loss, and out-of-band validation shrinks the window between corruption and discovery. Replication is not on this list: it copies corruption faithfully.
data-defense.out-of-band-validators: out-of-band validators, checksums, invariant checks → shrinks the window
data-defense.pitr-snapshots-cross-accoun: PITR, snapshots, cross-account copies → only real if restores are tested
data-defense.mark-hide-purge-after: mark, hide, purge after N days → catches user error and most app bugs
oncall-balance.cap: The %1% arithmetic: cap time %2% at a quarter of the week and incidents at two per shift, so every incident still has time for response, remediation and a %3%. A third incident is the one that gets no follow-up, which is why it recurs.
oncall-balance.fewer-than-one-incident: fewer than one incident per quarter is also a problem: skills rot
oncall-balance.3rd-event-no-time: 3rd event: no time to fix or write up
test-pyramid.cap: Testing for reliability spans traditional pre-production tests and tests that run against production. The higher the tier, the closer to reality and the more expensive each test becomes.
test-pyramid.cost-and-realism-rise: cost and realism rise with height
shuffle-sharding.cap: Shuffle sharding. With 8 nodes and 2-node shards there are 28 possible pairs, so customer C taking down both of its nodes leaves A and B with a healthy node each, and a retry succeeds. Only a customer assigned the identical pair is fully affected: one in 28.
shuffle-sharding.a-and-b-each: A and B each keep a healthy node · only an exact 3+7 shard fails
slo-window.cap: Rolling versus calendar windows. A calendar window resets the budget on the first of the month, which lines up with business reporting. A rolling window keeps an incident in view for exactly its length, which better reflects what users have recently experienced.
static-stability.cap: Static stability: the %1% keeps serving with what it already has, because nothing in the request path calls the %2%. The consequence is that you pre-provision enough capacity to survive losing an %3%, since scaling up during the event would need the %4% that is busiest right then.
static-stability.serves-with-what-exists: serves with what exists: running tasks, cached config, resolved %1%
static-stability.creates-and-changes-thi: creates and changes things: RunInstances, scaling, %1%, deployments
